% A second, deliberately tiny control — the ONLY reason it exists is that its
% multiple-answer question has THREE alternatives (#147 review, F1).
%
% `control-demo.tex`'s multiple has four, and so does every simple question's
% choice list, so `max` there is 4 for a multiple and 1 for a simple — which a
% reader could produce by hardcoding those two numbers and never reading AMC's
% own `max` column. That mutant was built and it passed the whole suite. The
% report's central promise is that `max` is the ALTERNATIVE COUNT and never a
% constant (ADR-0031), so one question has to prove it with a different count.
%
% It is a separate file rather than a thirteenth question in the shared pool
% because adding to that pool moves the seeded draw and re-points every
% expectation keyed to it — twice already in this WP.

\documentclass[letterpaper,11pt]{article}

\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}
\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}
\usepackage[spanish]{babel}
\usepackage[box,lang=ES]{automultiplechoice}

\def\unaSymbole{\textsf{\small(una respuesta)}}
\def\multiSymbole{\textsf{\small(varias respuestas)}}

\AMCrandomseed{1242}

\begin{document}

\element{clase}{
  \begin{questionmult}{tres-alternativas}
    ¿Cuáles de estas afirmaciones sobre un arreglo en Java son verdaderas?
    \begin{choices}
      \correctchoice{Su tamaño queda fijo al crearlo}
      \correctchoice{Sus posiciones se numeran desde 0}
      \wrongchoice{Crece solo al agregarle elementos}
    \end{choices}
  \end{questionmult}
}

\element{clase}{
  \begin{question}[\unaSymbole]{una-alternativa}
    En Java, ¿cuál de estos es un tipo primitivo?
    \begin{choices}
      \correctchoice{\texttt{int}}
      \wrongchoice{\texttt{String}}
      \wrongchoice{\texttt{Integer}}
    \end{choices}
  \end{question}
}

\onecopy{1}{

  \noindent{\large\bf Control de entrada}

  \begin{center}
    \emph{Marca tu RUT sin el dígito verificador (8 dígitos).}

    \AMCcode{rut}{8}
  \end{center}

  \insertgroup{clase}

  \AMCcleardoublepage
}

\end{document}
